reason: The sources provide over a dozen verified facts across seven independent outlets detailing Roman's origins, hardware, launch, and mission scope.
story: When NASA set out to map the dark cosmos, astronomers envisioned a modest infrared survey telescope. But in 2012, America's spy satellite agency, the National Reconnaissance Office, surprised NASA by handing over two classified 2.4-meter mirrors built for orbital surveillance. NASA adapted one of those reconnaissance optics into its next flagship observatory: the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after the agency's pioneering first chief of astronomy. Launched aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket in August 2026 to the Sun-Earth L2 point, Roman delivers the razor-sharp image resolution of the Hubble Space Telescope across a field of view 100 times wider. Over its first five years of science operations, Roman will scan more sky than Hubble imaged in over three decades. Armed with a 300-megapixel camera and a starlight-blocking coronagraph, it turns former spy hardware outward to trace dark energy and uncover thousands of hidden exoplanets.
angle: NASA built its next flagship observatory using a classified spy satellite mirror donated by the National Reconnaissance Office, matching Hubble's resolution across a field of view 100 times larger.

claims.claim: The telescope utilizes a 2.4-meter (7.9-foot) primary mirror.
The 2.4-meter primary mirror hardware was originally built for spy satellites and donated to NASA by the National Reconnaissance Office in 2012.
The observatory is named in honor of Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief of astronomy.
The telescope captures an image area 100 times larger than the imaging cameras on the Hubble Space Telescope.
Roman provides image sharpness and resolution comparable to the Hubble Space Telescope.
The mission was rated the top priority space mission for the 2020s by the 2010 Decadal Survey.
The observatory carries two science instruments: the Wide Field Instrument and the Coronagraph Instrument.
Roman launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
The telescope's operational destination is an orbit around the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, roughly 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
Congress allocated $90 million in the fiscal year 2016 omnibus spending bill to move the mission into formulation, far exceeding NASA's $14 million request.
Roman's prime scientific observation mission is slated to last five years.
Roman will use gravitational microlensing to discover thousands of distant and cold exoplanets.
The Coronagraph Instrument uses starlight suppression to enable direct imaging and spectroscopy of exoplanets.
Roman will probe dark energy and cosmic expansion by surveying thousands of distant Type Ia supernovae.

disputed: Field of view multiplier relative to Hubble: S1, S2, and S5 describe Roman's field of view as 100 times larger than Hubble's imaging cameras, while S4 cites 200 times Hubble's infrared view. The script should explicitly clarify it is 100 times larger than Hubble's standard imaging camera or up to 200 times its infrared view.

Prime mission duration: S1, S3, S4, and S6 specify a 5-year prime mission, whereas early reporting in S7 noted a prime mission of at least six years. The script should stick to the baselined five-year primary mission.

Cost effect of the donated NRO mirror: S5 reported that using the surplus mirror could be enlarged at no extra cost, while S1 stated the mirror's boundary conditions risked pushing total mission costs over a custom clean-sheet design. Scripts should avoid claiming the mirror made the total mission cheaper.
